summary: Massachusetts is one of the strictest states: before you can close on a one- or two-family home, the seller must have approved smoke alarms installed, and the local fire department must inspect the house for both smoke and carbon monoxide alarms and issue a Certificate of Compliance.
alarmType: What you need depends on when the house was built or permitted. Homes built or modified before Jan. 1, 1975 need alarms on every habitable level and in the basement, on the ceiling at the base of each stairway to a floor above, and outside each separate sleeping area; those alarms must be photoelectric (combination photoelectric/ionization or photoelectric/CO is allowed), may be battery or hardwired, and cannot be more than 10 years old or past the manufacturer's stated life. Any new or replacement alarm must be photoelectric, have a hush button, and if battery powered must use a 10-year sealed, non-rechargeable, non-replaceable battery. Homes permitted from 1975 onward follow the building code in force when the permit issued, which generally means hardwired interconnected alarms (with battery backup for permits after Aug. 27, 1997), plus an alarm inside every bedroom for post-1997 permits, and all-photoelectric hardwired interconnected alarms for permits on or after Feb. 4, 2011.
coAlarms: Required separately and also checked at sale. Since March 31, 2006 every residence with fossil-fuel-burning equipment (furnace, boiler, gas or oil water heater, fireplace, wood or pellet stove, gas dryer or range) or enclosed attached parking must have approved working CO alarms, whether or not it is being sold. On sale or transfer the fire chief must inspect for CO compliance. Placement is on every level including habitable basements and attics, within 10 feet of each bedroom door. Battery, plug-in with battery backup, hardwired with battery backup or system-type alarms are allowed in older homes; homes permitted on or after Jan. 1, 2008 need hardwired interconnected CO alarms with battery backup. Combination smoke/CO alarms are allowed but must give both a tone and a simulated voice to say which emergency it is.
certification: The head of the local fire department inspects and enforces, and issues a Certificate of Compliance after a passing inspection. Smoke and CO can be checked in the same visit; fees are set by each city or town, and the certificate is normally required at closing. The state fire marshal notes that even for post-1975 homes, where the sale law technically does not reach, most purchase and sale agreements and many mortgage lenders require the certificate anyway.
citation: Mass. G.L. c. 148, § 26F (smoke alarms on sale or transfer), § 26E (what alarms are required), § 26F1/2 (carbon monoxide alarms, inspection on sale); 527 CMR 1.00:13.7
notVerified: The malegislature.gov statute pages for c. 148 §§ 26E, 26F and 26F1/2 do not display an amendment history, so the date each section was last amended was not verified. The Department of Fire Services guide relied on for the alarm-type detail is dated December 1, 2016 (printed 11/18).

The text of 527 CMR 1.00:13.7 itself was not read directly; the photoelectric, 10-year sealed battery, hush-feature and CO placement details come from the Department of Fire Services' own guide (https://www.mass.gov/doc/consumer-guide-to-smoke-detectors-when-selling-home/download) rather than from the regulation text.
Section 26F applies to residential buildings of five units or fewer not covered by §§ 26A, 26B or 26C; the exact reach of those exclusions for unusual building types was not checked.
